question: If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ non-singular matrix such that $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$, prove that $(A^{-1})^{-1} = A$ and explain how this property defines the inverse uniquely.
explanation:
By definition of inverse, $AA^{-1} = I$.

Taking inverse again gives $(A^{-1})^{-1}A^{-1} = I$.

Thus $(A^{-1})^{-1}$ acts as the inverse of $A^{-1}$.

For square matrices the left and right inverse are the same, hence $(A^{-1})^{-1} = A$.

This also proves uniqueness: only the matrix $A$ satisfies the relation with $A^{-1}$, therefore the inverse of a matrix is unique.

options.B: $(A^{-1})^{-1}=I$ and every matrix has many inverses
options.C: $(A^{-1})^{-1}=A$ and this shows the inverse is unique
options.D: $(A^{-1})^{-1}=0$ and the inverse is unique only for singular matrices
